Done.

What I applied
- Canary Deployment (engine-v2-1) in canary-deployment-ns
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - same pod security configuration as stable (no special securityContext)

- Service update (recommendation-engine)
  - selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - now targets both stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods
  - port config unchanged (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Result
- With 2 replicas in stable and 2 in canary, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Kubernetes Services weight traffic by endpoint count; keeping both deployments at equal replica counts maintains ~50/50. If one side scales, the split will shift.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default; the Service continues to target 8080. The containerPort field is informational and was matched to the stable deployment (80), as requested.

Optional checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback
- To restore 100% to stable only: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I applied
- Canary Deployment (engine-v2-1) in canary-deployment-ns
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - same pod security configuration as stable (no special securityContext)

- Service update (recommendation-engine)
  - selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - now targets both stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods
  - port config unchanged (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Result
- With 2 replicas in stable and 2 in canary, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Kubernetes Services weight traffic by endpoint count; keeping both deployments at equal replica counts maintains ~50/50. If one side scales, the split will shift.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default; the Service continues to target 8080. The containerPort field is informational and was matched to the stable deployment (80), as requested.

Optional checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback
- To restore 100% to stable only: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

What I applied
- Canary Deployment (engine-v2-1) in canary-deployment-ns
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2

  - same pod security configuration as stable (no special securityContext)

- Service update (recommendation-engine)
  - selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - now targets both stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods
  - port config unchanged (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Result
- With 2 replicas in stable and 2 in canary, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

Notes
- Kubernetes Services weight traffic by endpoint count; keeping both deployments at equal replica counts maintains ~50/50. If one side scales, the split will shift.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default; the Service continues to target 8080. The containerPort field is informational and was matched to the stable deployment (80), as requested.

Optional checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback
- To restore 100% to stable only: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

outputSteps.content:
Fix complete.

What I found
- Root cause: The Deployment overrode the container command to run “/bin/sh -c nonexistent_command”, which doesn’t exist, causing CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the bad command/args so the container uses the image’s default entrypoint.
- Kept labels/selector (app=nginx) the same.
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
- Exposed containerPort 8080 (the unprivileged image listens on 8080).

Current status
- Pod app-6df8647c78-rmh4n is Running (1/1) in crashloop-test.
- Recent events show the new pod scheduled, pulled, created, and started successfully.

If you intended to run a custom command, replace it with a valid one (e.g., /usr/sbin/nginx -g 'daemon off;') or use a harmless placeholder like sleep infinity for debugging.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed it.

What I found
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass in your cluster).
- Dynamic provisioning created and bound a PV, allowing the pod to schedule.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns)
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (container nginx is running)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- PVC: homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO) to a dynamically provisioned volume.

Notes
- The “standard” StorageClass uses local-path (node-local) volumes with WaitForFirstConsumer, which is fine for RWO workloads like this.
- If you prefer the csi-hostpath-sc StorageClass instead, tell me and I’ll switch the PVC to that class.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I investigated and fixed it.

What I found
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass in your cluster).
- Dynamic provisioning created and bound a PV, allowing the pod to schedule.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns)
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (container nginx is running)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- PVC: homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO) to a dynamically provisioned volume.

Notes
- The “standard” StorageClass uses local-path (node-local) volumes with WaitForFirstConsumer, which is fine for RWO workloads like this.
- If you prefer the csi-hostpath-sc StorageClass instead, tell me and I’ll switch the PVC to that class.

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed it.

What I found
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass in your cluster).
- Dynamic provisioning created and bound a PV, allowing the pod to schedule.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns)
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (container nginx is running)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- PVC: homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO) to a dynamically provisioned volume.

Notes
- The “standard” StorageClass uses local-path (node-local) volumes with WaitForFirstConsumer, which is fine for RWO workloads like this.
- If you prefer the csi-hostpath-sc StorageClass instead, tell me and I’ll switch the PVC to that class.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and the probes were pointing to non‑existent endpoints (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and the service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left port 80 harmlessly declared; can remove if you want it cleaner).
- Service:
  - Kept Service port at 80, set targetPort to 8080 so consumers can still use port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available with 1/1 ready pod.
- Pod webapp-766b65d7bf-xgzvb is Ready 1/1.
- Service webapp has healthy endpoints pointing to 10.244.0.50:8080.

If you’d like this accessible from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress/LoadBalancer—just tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and the probes were pointing to non‑existent endpoints (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and the service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left port 80 harmlessly declared; can remove if you want it cleaner).
- Service:
  - Kept Service port at 80, set targetPort to 8080 so consumers can still use port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available with 1/1 ready pod.
- Pod webapp-766b65d7bf-xgzvb is Ready 1/1.
- Service webapp has healthy endpoints pointing to 10.244.0.50:8080.

If you’d like this accessible from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress/LoadBalancer—just tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and the probes were pointing to non‑existent endpoints (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and the service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left port 80 harmlessly declared; can remove if you want it cleaner).
- Service:
  - Kept Service port at 80, set targetPort to 8080 so consumers can still use port 80 inside the cluster.

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available with 1/1 ready pod.
- Pod webapp-766b65d7bf-xgzvb is Ready 1/1.
- Service webapp has healthy endpoints pointing to 10.244.0.50:8080.

If you’d like this accessible from outside the cluster, I can create an Ingress/LoadBalancer—just tell me the hostname or exposure method you prefer.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments and did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept existing permission to list apps/deployments.

Current binding
- RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader and Role pod-reader-role, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Expected: yes
- Or try listing: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you want, I can also generate a kubeconfig for the pod-reader SA so you can use it directly.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments and did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept existing permission to list apps/deployments.

Current binding
- RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader and Role pod-reader-role, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Expected: yes
- Or try listing: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you want, I can also generate a kubeconfig for the pod-reader SA so you can use it directly.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments and did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept existing permission to list apps/deployments.

Current binding
- RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader and Role pod-reader-role, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Expected: yes
- Or try listing: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you want, I can also generate a kubeconfig for the pod-reader SA so you can use it directly.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch 1: Service selector didn’t match pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
- Mismatch 2: Service targetPort didn’t match container port.
  - Container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080 (config shows listen 8080)
  - Service was targeting port 80

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and route to the right container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: 10.244.0.51:8080 for Service web/nginx
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080 and the pod IP
- HTTP request to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ returns the nginx welcome page

Next steps (if you need external access)
- Current Service type is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). Choose one:
  - Quick test: kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort: expose on each node’s IP and a nodePort
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud/LB)
  - Ingress: create an Ingress pointing to svc/nginx:80 (backed by an Ingress Controller)

Want me to set up NodePort, LoadBalancer, or an Ingress for external access?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch 1: Service selector didn’t match pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
- Mismatch 2: Service targetPort didn’t match container port.
  - Container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080 (config shows listen 8080)
  - Service was targeting port 80

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and route to the right container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: 10.244.0.51:8080 for Service web/nginx
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080 and the pod IP
- HTTP request to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ returns the nginx welcome page

Next steps (if you need external access)
- Current Service type is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). Choose one:
  - Quick test: kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort: expose on each node’s IP and a nodePort
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud/LB)
  - Ingress: create an Ingress pointing to svc/nginx:80 (backed by an Ingress Controller)

Want me to set up NodePort, LoadBalancer, or an Ingress for external access?

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a node selector that didn’t match any node. Events showed: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but your cluster has no node with that label.
- Effect: No pods -> Service web-app-service had no endpoints -> connection refused to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-l66zf: Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.53
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-7r7zn: Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.54
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service now has endpoints at 10.244.0.53:80 and 10.244.0.54:80
- Container logs show nginx started successfully.

This should clear the “connection refused” errors from the frontend because the backend service now has healthy endpoints.

If you actually need to constrain scheduling
- Option A (label a node to match the selector): Label the intended nodes and then re-add the selector.
  - Example: kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- Option B (use a different selector): Change nodeSelector to match real labels you use for your worker nodes (e.g., environment=production).
- Option C (taints/tolerations): If you taint special nodes, add matching tolerations instead of or in addition to selectors.

Recommended hardening (optional)
- Add readiness/liveness probes so endpoints are added only after your app is ready.
- Set resource requests/limits to improve scheduling and stability.

arguments.resource:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a node selector that didn’t match any node. Events showed: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but your cluster has no node with that label.
- Effect: No pods -> Service web-app-service had no endpoints -> connection refused to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-l66zf: Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.53
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-7r7zn: Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.54
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service now has endpoints at 10.244.0.53:80 and 10.244.0.54:80
- Container logs show nginx started successfully.

This should clear the “connection refused” errors from the frontend because the backend service now has healthy endpoints.

If you actually need to constrain scheduling
- Option A (label a node to match the selector): Label the intended nodes and then re-add the selector.
  - Example: kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- Option B (use a different selector): Change nodeSelector to match real labels you use for your worker nodes (e.g., environment=production).
- Option C (taints/tolerations): If you taint special nodes, add matching tolerations instead of or in addition to selectors.

Recommended hardening (optional)
- Add readiness/liveness probes so endpoints are added only after your app is ready.
- Set resource requests/limits to improve scheduling and stability.

Want me to add probes and resource requests now, or to re-apply a nodeSelector that matches your environment?

results.taskOutput:
All requested multi-tenant dev environments have been created and secured. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: environment=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: environment=dev, shared=true
  - staging: environment=staging
  - prod: environment=prod

2) RBAC
- Service accounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit”):
  - RoleBinding namespace-owner in each dev-<user> namespace binding:
    - User <user> and ServiceAccount <user>-sa to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress from all these namespaces to kube-system CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53)
- Dev namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace Ingress/Egress
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits Egress to dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer traffic (no egress to other dev-* namespaces)
- dev-shared:
  - allow-same-namespace for internal communication
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows Ingress from namespaces labeled environment=dev AND access-scope=developer (i.e., dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces (optional symmetry; note dev namespaces still deny ingress from dev-shared so no backchannel is created)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny plus allow-same-namespace
  - DNS egress only
  - No dev namespace communication possible; dev namespaces cannot egress to staging/prod, and staging/prod do not allow ingress from others

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

Notes and next steps
- Least privilege: Developers have “edit” in their own namespaces (full workload management without RBAC admin). If you require true “admin” rights (ability to manage RBAC objects in their own namespace), say the word and I’ll switch those RoleBindings from edit to admin.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- “System services” currently interpreted as DNS. If workloads must also call the Kubernetes API from pods, we can add a small egress rule to the default/kubernetes service (TCP 443) in each namespace.

Everything above has been applied and is ready for use.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested multi-tenant dev environments have been created and secured. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: environment=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: environment=dev, shared=true
  - staging: environment=staging
  - prod: environment=prod

2) RBAC
- Service accounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit”):
  - RoleBinding namespace-owner in each dev-<user> namespace binding:
    - User <user> and ServiceAccount <user>-sa to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress from all these namespaces to kube-system CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53)
- Dev namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace Ingress/Egress
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits Egress to dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer traffic (no egress to other dev-* namespaces)
- dev-shared:
  - allow-same-namespace for internal communication
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows Ingress from namespaces labeled environment=dev AND access-scope=developer (i.e., dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces (optional symmetry; note dev namespaces still deny ingress from dev-shared so no backchannel is created)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny plus allow-same-namespace
  - DNS egress only
  - No dev namespace communication possible; dev namespaces cannot egress to staging/prod, and staging/prod do not allow ingress from others

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

Notes and next steps
- Least privilege: Developers have “edit” in their own namespaces (full workload management without RBAC admin). If you require true “admin” rights (ability to manage RBAC objects in their own namespace), say the word and I’ll switch those RoleBindings from edit to admin.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- “System services” currently interpreted as DNS. If workloads must also call the Kubernetes API from pods, we can add a small egress rule to the default/kubernetes service (TCP 443) in each namespace.

Everything above has been applied and is ready for use.

- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: environment=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: environment=dev, shared=true
  - staging: environment=staging
  - prod: environment=prod

2) RBAC
- Service accounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace (least-privilege “edit”):
  - RoleBinding namespace-owner in each dev-<user> namespace binding:
    - User <user> and ServiceAccount <user>-sa to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress from all these namespaces to kube-system CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53)
- Dev namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace Ingress/Egress
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits Egress to dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer traffic (no egress to other dev-* namespaces)
- dev-shared:
  - allow-same-namespace for internal communication
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows Ingress from namespaces labeled environment=dev AND access-scope=developer (i.e., dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces (optional symmetry; note dev namespaces still deny ingress from dev-shared so no backchannel is created)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny plus allow-same-namespace
  - DNS egress only
  - No dev namespace communication possible; dev namespaces cannot egress to staging/prod, and staging/prod do not allow ingress from others

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

Notes and next steps
- Least privilege: Developers have “edit” in their own namespaces (full workload management without RBAC admin). If you require true “admin” rights (ability to manage RBAC objects in their own namespace), say the word and I’ll switch those RoleBindings from edit to admin.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- “System services” currently interpreted as DNS. If workloads must also call the Kubernetes API from pods, we can add a small egress rule to the default/kubernetes service (TCP 443) in each namespace.

Everything above has been applied and is ready for use.

Steps.message:
Done.

What I created and did:
- Namespace statefulset-test
- Headless Service db (for stable network IDs)
- StatefulSet db with 3 replicas:
  - Each pod mounts a 1Gi PersistentVolumeClaim at /data
  - An init container writes the file /data/test with the string initial_data on first boot
- Scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica

Verification:
- Current pods: db-0 is Running (db-1 and db-2 have been terminated)
- /data/test in db-0 contains: initial_data (12 bytes)

Notes:
- PVCs for db-1 and db-2 were retained when scaling down, so they still contain initial_data and will reattach with their data if you scale back up.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of troubleshooting and fix (vm-troubleshoot flow)

What I checked
- VirtualMachine (kubevirt.io/v1) broken-vm: printableStatus was “Starting”; volumes included cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef name vm-cloud-init.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm: initially stuck in Scheduling/Pending; a virt-launcher pod was created but not progressing.
- virt-launcher pod events: Warning FailedMount — “secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”
- Secret vm-cloud-init: did not exist in vm-test-troubleshoot namespace.

Root cause
- The VM referenced a non-existent cloud-init Secret (vm-cloud-init). The missing Secret caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume, leaving the VM stuck during initialization.

Action taken to fix
- Created the vm-cloud-init Secret in vm-test-troubleshoot with cloud-init user data. I included both keys (userdata and userData) to satisfy the pod’s subPath mounts.
- Re-checked pod/VMI status and events to confirm progress.

Verification and current status
- After creating the Secret, the virt-launcher pod initialized successfully.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm transitioned to phase Running; condition Ready=True.
- Reported pod network IP: 10.244.0.91.

Details
- Error observed: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found (virt-launcher-broken-vm-84j28 event).
- Fix applied: Created Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal cloud-init:
  - user: fedora, password set, ssh_pwauth: true (for quick validation). Note: rotate/remove this credential as appropriate.

Outcome
- Fix was successful. The VM is now running and Ready.

Follow-ups and recommendations
- If you need guest details from inside the VM (OS/filesystems/ips/users), install and enable qemu-guest-agent in the guest, then we can query it.
- Consider replacing the temporary password-based cloud-init with SSH keys and disabling password auth for security.

InterfaceNotLiveMigratable: cannot migrate VMI which does not use masquerade or a migratable plugin to connect to the pod network

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Summary of troubleshooting and fix (vm-troubleshoot flow)

What I checked
- VirtualMachine (kubevirt.io/v1) broken-vm: printableStatus was “Starting”; volumes included cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef name vm-cloud-init.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm: initially stuck in Scheduling/Pending; a virt-launcher pod was created but not progressing.
- virt-launcher pod events: Warning FailedMount — “secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”
- Secret vm-cloud-init: did not exist in vm-test-troubleshoot namespace.

Root cause
- The VM referenced a non-existent cloud-init Secret (vm-cloud-init). The missing Secret caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume, leaving the VM stuck during initialization.

Action taken to fix
- Created the vm-cloud-init Secret in vm-test-troubleshoot with cloud-init user data. I included both keys (userdata and userData) to satisfy the pod’s subPath mounts.
- Re-checked pod/VMI status and events to confirm progress.

Verification and current status
- After creating the Secret, the virt-launcher pod initialized successfully.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm transitioned to phase Running; condition Ready=True.
- Reported pod network IP: 10.244.0.91.

Details
- Error observed: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found (virt-launcher-broken-vm-84j28 event).
- Fix applied: Created Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal cloud-init:
  - user: fedora, password set, ssh_pwauth: true (for quick validation). Note: rotate/remove this credential as appropriate.

Outcome
- Fix was successful. The VM is now running and Ready.

Follow-ups and recommendations
- If you need guest details from inside the VM (OS/filesystems/ips/users), install and enable qemu-guest-agent in the guest, then we can query it.
- Consider replacing the temporary password-based cloud-init with SSH keys and disabling password auth for security.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of troubleshooting and fix (vm-troubleshoot flow)

What I checked
- VirtualMachine (kubevirt.io/v1) broken-vm: printableStatus was “Starting”; volumes included cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef name vm-cloud-init.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm: initially stuck in Scheduling/Pending; a virt-launcher pod was created but not progressing.
- virt-launcher pod events: Warning FailedMount — “secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”
- Secret vm-cloud-init: did not exist in vm-test-troubleshoot namespace.

Root cause
- The VM referenced a non-existent cloud-init Secret (vm-cloud-init). The missing Secret caused the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume, leaving the VM stuck during initialization.

Action taken to fix
- Created the vm-cloud-init Secret in vm-test-troubleshoot with cloud-init user data. I included both keys (userdata and userData) to satisfy the pod’s subPath mounts.
- Re-checked pod/VMI status and events to confirm progress.

Verification and current status
- After creating the Secret, the virt-launcher pod initialized successfully.
- VirtualMachineInstance broken-vm transitioned to phase Running; condition Ready=True.
- Reported pod network IP: 10.244.0.91.

Details
- Error observed: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found (virt-launcher-broken-vm-84j28 event).
- Fix applied: Created Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal cloud-init:
  - user: fedora, password set, ssh_pwauth: true (for quick validation). Note: rotate/remove this credential as appropriate.

Outcome
- Fix was successful. The VM is now running and Ready.

Follow-ups and recommendations
- If you need guest details from inside the VM (OS/filesystems/ips/users), install and enable qemu-guest-agent in the guest, then we can query it.
- Consider replacing the temporary password-based cloud-init with SSH keys and disabling password auth for security.

  - Interface: default, MAC 4a:3e:5d:d3:94:e3, IP 10.244.0.92 (infoSource=domain)

What guest agent data would typically include
- OS info:
  - Name, pretty name, version, kernel release and version, machine/architecture, timezone/UTC offset
- Filesystems:
  - Devices and mountpoints, filesystem type, total/used/free bytes
- Network interfaces:
  - Interface names, MAC addresses, assigned IPv4/IPv6 addresses, possibly MTU
- Users:
  - List of currently logged-in users (name, terminal/tty, login time, remote host)

Next steps to get guest agent data
- Inside the VM:
  - Ensure qemu-guest-agent is installed and running:
    - Fedora/RHEL: sudo dnf install -y qemu-guest-agent; sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
    - Check: systemctl status qemu-guest-agent
  - Give it 1–2 minutes after boot/cloud-init for the service to start.
- On the cluster:
  - Ensure the KubeVirt subresource API is available (virt-api healthy, CRDs/aggregated API for subresources.kubevirt.io present).
- I can retry fetching the guest agent info on your signal. If you’d like, I can keep polling until data appears.
